schools.summary: Gill takes the tribute to gather in all the king's dominions (Aben Ezra: peoples in fear, not under his rule), and guesses the levy came of Xerxes' Greek wars or of taxes remitted at his marriage to Esther.
Henry reads the tribute as the measure of a vast dominion and revenue, an additional levy beyond the usual customs (Ezra 4:13), with a patriot's aside on free versus arbitrary taxation.
Clarke sets the tribute on the 127 provinces and the isles of the Aegean, conquered by Darius Hystaspes, whom Calmet takes for the Ahasuerus of Esther.
Ellicott reads the levy as the aftermath of the ruinous Greek expedition and the war still dragging on near Asia Minor; Cyprus alone remained to Persia, the Aegean now free.

debates.question: Which Persian king is the Ahasuerus of this book?

sides.position: Xerxes, whose Greek wars fit the demand for fresh tribute
Darius Hystaspes, who conquered the Aegean isles

debates.question: What are 'the isles of the sea'?

sides.position: Cyprus, the Aegean being by now free of Persian rule and the phrase only retained by habit

schools.summary: Clarke notes the Persians' exact chronicles (their Tareekhs, numerous still); Wesley looks past them to their vanishing, the records lost while the sacred writings endure as the days of heaven.

Henry presses the contrast: the Persian chronicles long lost, while the sacred writings live till time shall be no more (Ps. 9:6; Dan. 2:44), the despised worshippers deemed by the Holy Spirit greater than the mightiest monarch.
Gill notes only that Xerxes was a very mighty and powerful prince, whose acts filled the royal annals.
Ellicott adds a philological touch: 'power' is the same word rendered 'authority' at Esther 9:29.

themes: the chronicles of Media and Persia
the kingdom of God as the days of heaven

schools.summary: Henry gives the fullest portrait, dividing the verse into greatness and goodness: Mordecai owned his people, sought not his own wealth, and was a common father speaking peace to all.

Clarke enlarges the office (prime minister and governor of the empire), relays the Targum's extravagant encomium, and marks where the Hebrew text ends and the Greek and Vulgate add the apocryphal chapters.
Ellicott sets Mordecai at his zenith about 470 B.C. and leaves his end uncertain (Artabanus chief adviser, Xerxes murdered 464 B.C.), the last view a loyal benefactor seeking his people's weal.
Gill states the plain dignity: Mordecai was next unto the king, second in the kingdom, the prime minister of state.

outliers.note: Sets Mordecai's greatness in secular history and leaves its close in shadow: at the end of Xerxes' reign the chief adviser was Artabanus, not Mordecai, so his eminence may not have lasted.

themes: seeking the wealth of his people
the Hebrew text ends and the apocryphal additions
